Pre-Socratic Philosophy. This encompasses the Greek natural philosophers who were active before or at the same time as Socrates, roughly from 470 to 399 BCE. They sought rational explanations for the nature of reality, change, and being. These thinkers, including the Milesians, the Pythagoreans, Heraclitus, and Parmenides, abandoned mythological accounts and pioneered Western logic, metaphysics, and natural science. Though their works survive only in fragments and later quotations, they established the foundational problems and methods that defined philosophy for the next 2,400 years.

The earliest Pre-Socratic thinkers were the Milesians: Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes. They sought a single underlying substance from which all reality arises. Thales argued it was water, Anaximander proposed the apeiron, which means the infinite or boundless, and Anaximenes said it was air. Pythagoras founded a religious and philosophical community emphasizing the mystical importance of number and geometry. Pythagorean harmonies influenced music theory and cosmology for centuries to come.

Heraclitus taught that reality is in constant flux and that fire is the underlying principle. He emphasized the paradoxical unity of opposites and the logos governing change. Parmenides argued the opposite: that reality must be eternal, unchanging, and indivisible, and that change and plurality are illusions. This thesis challenged the evidence of the senses and provoked centuries of philosophical response. Zeno of Elea devised famous paradoxes—Achilles and the tortoise, the arrow—to defend Parmenidean monism by exposing contradictions in accepting plurality and motion.

The Atomists, Leucippus and Democritus, resolved the tension between Parmenides and Heraclitus by proposing that indivisible atoms move in void, thereby explaining change and multiplicity without violating Parmenidean logic. Pre-Socratic thinkers pioneered the demand for natural, non-mythological causes and rational argument, establishing the epistemic norms that define Western philosophy. Socrates later redirected philosophy toward human ethics and knowledge, marking a watershed in how Western thinkers approached fundamental questions about the world and our place in it.
